newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE - Colombia fights ongoing battle with broca.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE - Colombia fights ongoing battle with broca.

text.p: Eight years after it invaded the country from neighboring Ecuador, Colombia continues to wage war against a tiny black beetle responsible for a plague known as "broca" that has infected more than half of its coffee farms.
It is a war that threatens to continue without end since the beetle, no bigger than the head of a pin, has proven to be virtually impossible to eradicate.

Officials with the National Coffee Growers' Federation have claimed some success in fighting the beetle, however, even though they say it has earned a well-deserved place alongside the cockroaches, rats and other vermin that will eventually inherit the earth.
Problems caused by the berry borer, so-called because it eats its way inside coffee berries while thay are still on the tree, are manageable even if they will never go away, the officials say.
"The damage done today is less than before, there's no doubt about that," John Naranjo, the federation's commercial manager told Reuters in a recent interview.
According to the Growers' Federation, the percentage of crops infested by broca has actually dropped, even as the plague continues to spread.

In September 1993, the infestation was detected on 329,238 hectares of the country's total coffee plantations, an area covering 1.1 million hectares. That number jumped to 653,000 hectares in September of this year.

But Almacafe -- the company responsible for transporting and storing the coffee the federation purchases from growers in 15 provinces across Colombia -- says the percentage of crops infested by the berry borer dropped from 12 percent in the first half of 1995 to six percent as of May 1996.
Of the 12 million 60-kilo bags of coffee Colombia produces on average every year, about 1.5 million show the ravages of the berry borer, Gonzalo Rivera, Almacafe's manager said in an interview.
"It's one thing for everyone to have a fever, but it's something else again when some have a 40 (104 Fahrenheit) and others have a 38 (100F)," he said.

In other words, the berry borer may have spread steadily in recent years, but the federation -- which spent $10 million fighting broca this year alone -- has managed to limit its destructive capabilities through a nationwide advertising campaign ensuring that growers know how to keep it under control.

Growers have complained about the high costs of insecticides and manual labor associated with the anti-broca fight, with some estimating that it has increased production costs by at least 10 percent a year.

And some exporters say there has been a recent increase in the amount of coffee infected with broca coming from the southern provinces of Huila, Narino and Cauca, prompting them to halt all purchases from those areas.

The federation guarantees purchases of the infected coffee at a discount and either stockpiles or sells it for internal consumption. Industry sources say some of it -- which can produce a bitter aftertaste because it needs to be roasted longer than normal beans -- is making its way into export markets, however.
Broca is not exclusive to Colombia. But one leading exporter said its farmers have learned to live with it better than in other countries and it no longer poses the threat it once did.
"They're winning the war," he said, even though a stalemate looks far more certain than a victory against broca anytime soon.
